question: Na vysokohorskej chate, napríklad pod Rysmi, sa vajce natvrdo varí dlhšie ako doma v nížine, hoci voda v hrnci rovnako bublá. Prečo?
source_excerpt: At higher elevations, where the atmospheric pressure is much lower, the boiling point is also lower.

extra.why_interesting: People assume boiling water is always equally hot, so a mountain hut egg taking longer seems odd. The player can reason out the answer from the familiar idea that air gets thinner higher up.
extra.verification_notes: Lower atmospheric pressure at altitude lowers water's boiling point, so eggs cook more slowly; this is confirmed by https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boiling_point.

explanation: Pri nižšom tlaku vzduchu voda vrie skôr, vo výške okolo 2250 metrov už asi pri 92 °C, takže vajce sa varí v chladnejšej vode, než si myslíme.

question: V treskúcom mraze sneh pod topánkami vŕzga, no pri teplote okolo nuly sa v ňom kráča úplne potichu. Čo sa v tom mrazivom snehu deje, že vydáva taký zvuk?
source_excerpt: When the snow is colder than -10C, the pressure from your boot does not melt the snow, and instead the ice crystals beneath your boot are crushed making a squeaking

extra.why_interesting: Every Slovak has heard snow squeak on a frosty morning but assumes it is just 'the sound of cold'. The real cause is mechanical. In hard frost no lubricating water layer forms, so millions of tiny crystals break, and you are hearing them crack.
extra.verification_notes: Squeaking in very cold snow is attributed to crushed or fractured ice crystals, while near-0 °C snow has a liquid film or melts under pressure and is silent; sources differ slightly on mechanism but agree on crystal fracture/grinding.

explanation: Pri silnom mraze, zhruba pod mínus desať stupňov, sa kryštáliky pod nohou nestihnú natopiť na tenkú vrstvičku vody, ktorá by ich premazala. Namiesto toho praskajú a trú sa o seba a tie tisíce drobných prasknutí počujeme ako vŕzganie.
